:question/problem:
Which of the following gives the arc length of the curve defined by

$$
x=t,\qquad y=e^t,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$

The indicated segment is shown below.

![Parametric curve segment with direction and parameter endpoints](images/9d/9d6b750b612ea841f5afb9bc37ed3d774d3051c77a13e2cb691218c051b1d3b6.png)

Use the arc-length formula

$$
L=\int_a^b\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Choose an integral expression. Do not evaluate it.
:question/worked-solution:
For a parametric curve, use

$$
L=\int_a^b\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t$, we obtain

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}=1,\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}=e^t.
$$

Substitute the derivatives and the parameter limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\int_0^1\sqrt{1^2+(e^t)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t\\&=\int_0^1\sqrt{1+e^{2t}}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Square each derivative and add the squares inside the square root. In particular, $(e^t)^2=e^{2t}$. The integration limits are the given parameter values, $0$ and $1$. This integral is the requested expression; no evaluation is needed.

:question/problem:
Which of the following gives the arc length of the curve defined by

$$
x=\sin(2t)-1,\qquad y=\cos(3t)+2,\qquad 0\le t\le\frac{\pi}{3}.
$$

The indicated segment is shown below.

![Parametric curve segment with direction and parameter endpoints](images/39/397d64be37483a28368c36a7bef340c511c9aff9a7e6160e727ba71ea22a18d5.png)

Choose an integral expression. Do not evaluate it.
:question/worked-solution:
For a parametric curve, use

$$
L=\int_a^b\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t$, we obtain

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}=2\cos(2t),\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}=-3\sin(3t).
$$

Substitute the derivatives and the parameter limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\int_0^{\pi/3}\sqrt{(2\cos(2t))^2+(-3\sin(3t))^2}\,\mathrm{d}t\\&=\int_0^{\pi/3}\sqrt{4\cos^2(2t)+9\sin^2(3t)}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

The constants $-1$ and $2$ have zero derivatives. The chain rule supplies factors $2$ and $3$, which become $4$ and $9$ when squared. Squaring the negative derivative gives a positive term. The arguments $2t$ and $3t$ differ, so the two squared trigonometric terms cannot be combined using the Pythagorean identity. Keep the parameter limits $0$ and $\pi/3$ and leave the integral unevaluated.

:question/problem:
Which of the following gives the arc length of the curve defined by

$$
x=e^t,\qquad y=e^t\cos t,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$

The indicated segment is shown below.

![Parametric curve segment with direction and parameter endpoints](images/38/38d4840253365e13b08d93e0cfcf2194e759cb95d7b7fda9ceaec3805dd5556f.png)

Choose an integral expression. Do not evaluate it.
:question/worked-solution:
For a parametric curve, use

$$
L=\int_a^b\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Applying the product rule to $y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}&=e^t,\\\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}&=e^t\cos t-e^t\sin t=e^t(\cos t-\sin t).\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the derivatives and the parameter limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\int_0^1\sqrt{e^{2t}+e^{2t}(\cos t-\sin t)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t\\&=\int_0^1 e^t\sqrt{1+\cos^2t+\sin^2t-2\sin t\cos t}\,\mathrm{d}t\\&=\int_0^1 e^t\sqrt{2-\sin(2t)}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $y$ requires the product rule. In simplifying the speed, use $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$ and $2\sin t\cos t=\sin(2t)$. Also, $\sqrt{e^{2t}}=e^t$ because $e^t>0$. Thus the constant inside the final square root is $2$, and the cross term has a minus sign. Leave the integral unevaluated.
